summary: Suggests an experimental way to run the Network Time Protocol over the OSI Remote Operations Service, so hosts in either the OSI or Internet communities can synchronize time.

eli5.summary: Computers that use a different kind of messaging can still ask each other the time. This shows how.

questions: network time protocol remote operations service
how does ntp work over osi
can ntp run over connection-oriented networks
subtitle: Running NTP over the OSI Remote Operations Service instead of UDP.

tldr.problem: Network Time Protocol runs over UDP, but OSI applications need time synchronization too, and some networks use connection-oriented services like X.25 instead of UDP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC shows how to adapt NTP to run over OSI Remote Operations Service (ROS), which provides a connection-oriented interface and allows NTP daemons to peer using explicit connection establishment.
tldr.outcome: Prototype implementations show the approach works reliably over X.25, and offers the possibility of using connection success to optimize reachability discovery.

today: RFC 1165 is an Experimental document that was never standardized. While it demonstrated the feasibility of running NTP over OSI-based transports, Internet-based time synchronization using NTP over UDP remained the dominant approach.

sections.title: Running NTP Over OSI
sections.content:
This RFC describes how to implement the Network Time Protocol over an ISO OSI stack, specifically using the Remote Operations Service (ROS) rather than UDP. NTP itself is documented in RFC 1119.

While NTP was originally designed for the Internet using UDP, it is also needed by OSI applications. The challenge is that OSI typically uses connection-oriented services like X.25 rather than connectionless UDP.
sections.eli5: Computers that speak OSI need to tell time to each other, just like Internet computers do. This explains how to make NTP work in that world.

sections.title: Why Use Remote Operations Service
sections.content:
There are four main reasons to implement NTP over ROS. First, it provides a useful time synchronization service to the OSI community. Second, ROS and ASN.1 specifications can be automatically checked and have code generated from them, making implementation easier. Third, NTP can run over connection-oriented services, and connection success or failure can directly determine reachability instead of relying on shift registers.

Fourth, using ROS makes NTP independent of the underlying communications architecture. Time synchronization is critical for OSI applications: for example, X.511 authentication relies on encrypted packets with time stamps. If two hosts have unsynchronized clocks, the host with the faster clock becomes vulnerable to cryptographic attacks.
sections.eli5: Connecting like a phone call instead of sending a postcard has advantages: you know right away if the other computer is there, and you do not have to keep resending the same information.

sections.title: Protocol Overview and Connection States
sections.content:
The NTP application functions exactly as RFC 1119 defines it. NTP daemons peer with one another by sending an A-ASSOCIATE.REQUEST and receiving an A-ASSOCIATE.INDICATION. On successful association, they periodically invoke the appropriate Remote Operation with the correct parameters at the appropriate frequency. On failure, they mark the peer as unreachable.

The ROS-based implementation adds new states for each peer: Connected (the host is connected and exchanging synchronization data), Connecting (a connection is in progress), Accepting (a connection is being accepted but negotiation is not yet complete), and Disconnected (the remote host cannot be contacted).
sections.eli5: When using a phone call, you dial the other computer to connect. While connected, you can check the time whenever you want. If the call does not go through, you know the computer is not available.

sections.title: Simplified Data Format
sections.content:
With a connection-oriented service, the NTP packet can be simplified. In standard NTP over UDP, every packet must include all necessary information: synchronization data, authentication data, and protocol data such as version and clock precision. But on an established connection, some of this information does not change across multiple exchanges.

Authentication (if used) needs to be done at connection establishment but not necessarily for every packet. Protocol version and local clock precision are unlikely to vary over the lifetime of the connection. The ROS-based NTP therefore removes this redundant information from the basic packet, keeping only the synchronization data (timestamps, stratum, and clock offsets).
sections.eli5: On a phone call with the same person, you do not have to introduce yourself every time you speak. NTP over ROS works the same way.

sections.title: Network Properties and Prototype Results
sections.content:
An important insight for time synchronization is that high network speed is less important than the consistency of packet transit times. A low-speed network with little variance in transit times produces better results than a high-speed network with large variations. This suggests that connection-oriented networks with resource allocation at connection time might actually provide better accuracy than connectionless networks, which can suffer large swings in transit time under high load.

Prototype implementations from UK sites show promising results. Sites running NTP over ROS over X.25 achieved similar reliability to the UDP model. These prototypes successfully peered both over ROS with UK sites on X.25 and over UDP with US Internet sites, demonstrating interoperability across different transport mechanisms.
sections.eli5: A steady slow road is better for telling time than a fast road with traffic jams. Connection-oriented networks are more steady.
